slides.title: Can better handoffs make an RLM more reliable?
slides.notes:
SAY: Last time, we taught a basic Python routine, but reliable helper use remained open. Today adds a harder training result and a study of how helper answers return to their source records.

FOCUS: Can changing the RLM's surrounding program make complete solutions more reliable?

CAUTION: The old and new training tests are different tasks, not points on one progress curve.

slides.title: A long file can become many small questions whose answers Python can combine.
slides.notes:
SAY: Follow one example. A file holds many users' questions. The main model asks helpers which questions concern places, then Python combines those replies into user totals. It can inspect the result and continue.

WHY: An unfamiliar whole may become familiar smaller steps.

CAUTION: This motivates RLMs; our experiments do not demonstrate general autonomous planning or deep recursion.

slides.title: Training taught a more reliable routine for asking helpers and calculating answers.
slides.notes:
SAY: Worked examples taught what action to take next, not just the final number. On 72 shared questions, verified successes were 12 before this training and 55 or 53 afterward.

IF ASKED: Missing outcomes allow 12–19, 55, and 53–55. The two trained copies used different example sets, not sequential training.

CAUTION: Familiar question types; the helper remained fixed.

slides.title: We changed how helper answers are linked to the text they describe.
slides.notes:
SAY: Maya bought a red bike. The first statement is supported; the second is contradicted. Repeat an arbitrary name beside each statement and its answer, so they can be matched explicitly.

IF ASKED: Software fixed names and format, but not the reading answers. The unnamed version relies on list position.

TRANSITION: Does this small interface change matter when many questions are answered together?

slides.title: Matching names improved accuracy when a helper answered many questions at once.
slides.notes:
SAY: Read left to right as each call handles more questions. At 64, names raised Qwen from 44% to 83%, and Mistral from 35% to 52%.

IF ASKED: Same 16 record sets; 160 calls per model shown. Three malformed Mistral named outputs count wrong, not missing.

CAUTION: These are helper answers, not complete RLM solutions. Full three-format results are backup 6.

slides.title: Smaller calls were faster than large named calls in this local test.
slides.notes:
SAY: All methods handled the same 768 questions. Large named calls scored 85% in 91 seconds; single-question calls scored 87% in 31 seconds.

IF ASKED: Four calls ran concurrently, even for single-question requests. Sixteen-question calls were faster but less accurate. Startup is excluded.

CAUTION: Single-question calls sent about 2.5 times as many input tokens as large named calls. Local speed is not universal cost.

slides.title: Proposed RLM change: manage record links and make helper group size an explicit choice.
slides.notes:
SAY: Let the RLM program manage record-level groups and returned answers. Then test complete solutions against the current RLM and simpler small-call baselines at a fixed budget.

IF ASKED: Current ask_batch aligns whole requests. This adds individual-record handling inside requests. Learning when to resize groups is a later step.

CAUTION: This component is proposed. IDs are standard, and correct matching cannot guarantee true reading answers.

slides.title: We have a promising handoff result and a focused next research question.
slides.notes:
SAY: Training improved a routine; matching names improved helper reading. I recommend a focused whole-task study of the handoff procedure.

DISCUSS: Is this a worthwhile contribution? Which realistic task would make a convincing test?

STOP: This ends the ten-minute main talk. Remaining slides are optional answers to questions, not more required presentation.

slides.title: Example: the helper reads the text, and Python does the counting.
slides.notes:
SAY: Ada's place-question weights total seven; Ben's total two. Only Ada exceeds five, so the answer is one user.

IF ASKED: The model learns actions that query helpers and calculate from their real replies. Wrong helper labels can spoil correct arithmetic.

CAUTION: These four rows are an illustration, not a copied training example. The weights are artificial values, not confidence.

slides.title: A control suggests that matching matters, not merely having names on the page.
slides.notes:
SAY: Both versions had names, but only one reused the same names on both sides. Accuracy on later answers rose from 32.6% to 78.8%, with valid formatting throughout.

IF ASKED: Position still specified which record to answer; different names did not instruct a different task.

CAUTION: Different input panel from main slide 5. This supports matching as a factor, not an internal-mechanism claim.

slides.title: Reward training did not improve the final-answer count in this trial.
slides.notes:
SAY: Longer reward runs did not improve final-answer counts: 57 before, 55–57 with answer reward, and 54 with an extra calculation check.

IF ASKED: Each attempted 576 solutions; 19 and 21 updates actually used informative groups. Together they took about four hours and 39 minutes.

CAUTION: This scores final numbers, unlike slide 3. Full calculation review is pending; it does not disprove reward learning.

slides.title: Training also helped with new combinations of familiar steps.
slides.notes:
SAY: The trained model executed new combinations more often: two verified successes before training, 29 afterward, out of 72.

EXAMPLE: Find users who asked about places, then count their questions asking for numbers. The prompt explicitly gave these two steps.

CAUTION: Missing results allow 2–13 versus 29–30. Many correct answers were zero, so we checked actual calculations. This is not autonomous planning.

slides.title: Misleading names can draw an answer toward the wrong input.
slides.notes:
SAY: If row 7's answer box carries row 8's name, the model may answer the wrong record. Accuracy was 39% with misleading visible-row names and 80% with names pointing nowhere visible.

CAUTION: This was deliberately misleading input, not normal deployment. We observed behavior, not attention or the model's internal mechanism.

slides.title: Both row numbers and arbitrary names helped in the larger-batch tests.
slides.notes:
SAY: The main plot omitted row numbers for clarity, not because they failed. Both row numbers and arbitrary matching names helped.

IF ASKED: All 480 calls returned. Three malformed Mistral arbitrary-name outputs count wrong. Those failures confound a direct semantic comparison between name types.

CAUTION: Matching helps but does not remove all errors or prove a speed advantage.
